title: Audit Steward Playbook — Customer-Managed Network Quickdraft
body:
Purpose:

This quickdraft introduces the "Audit Steward" concept: a lightweight orchestration and evidence-packaging layer that sits between Redwood-managed control-plane actions and customer-managed networking (VPCs, on-prem gateways). The steward's goal is to make approvals and audit logs compact, verifiable, and legally portable while keeping customer data under their residency/KMS constraints.

Intended audience:
- Product & PM for Private deployments
- Eng (private-deployments, infra, observability)
- Solutions & SRE for pilot customers

Background / problem we solve:
- Customers require cryptographically verifiable proof that a control-plane change occurred and what artifacts were exchanged during handoff (config blobs, cert rotations, NAT rules).
- Existing audit log exports are large, unstructured, and often store PII (headers, IPs) that customers can't allow Redwood to persist long-term.
- Approval gates today are manual or monolithic; they don't produce a compact evidence bundle that can be re-played for forensic or compliance purposes.

High-level proposal:
- Introduce an "Audit Steward" service (lightweight process inside private control plane) that:
  - Creates an immutable, compressed 'evidence capsule' per network-change transaction.
  - Attaches a minimal structured audit-record (see schema below) and signs it with Redwood's signing key.
  - Optionally requests a customer-side co-signature via their KMS/HSM (async) before marking change as "attested".
  - Provides sampling and minimization: redact or trim any fields marked as 'customer-sensitive' by policy config.
  - Supplies replay helpers (manifest + pointers) that solutions teams can use to reconstruct the change in a forensics environment.

Goals / success metrics:
- Pilot with 3 regulated customers within 10 weeks.
- Produce evidence capsule <= 1 MB for 90% of routine VPC handoffs.
- Enable automated policy-based blacklisting/redaction of PII fields (target 100% coverage for standard headers).
- Reduce manual investigator time per incident by 40% (measured via support ticket sampling).

User stories:
- As a solutions engineer, I want a compact, verifiable artifact I can send to a customer so they can independently verify a network change without sharing whole logs.
- As a security reviewer at a customer, I want the control-plane change signed by my KMS before I allow traffic to shift.
- As an operator, I want an approval gate that can be configured for different escalation policies (auto-approve for low-risk, multi-signer for high-risk).

Audit record schema (minimal, JSON-serializable):
- transaction_id: uuid
- timestamp_utc: iso8601
- initiator: principal (redwood:user/service or customer:operator)
- scope: [resource identifiers] (e.g., vpc-id, gateway-id)
- delta_hash: sha256 of canonical-change-payload
- capsule_ref: signed-pointer (storage://path or short proof blob)
- retention_hint: policy-id
- signatures: [redwood-signature, optional-customer-kms-signature-id]
- sampling_note: (why this was sampled or fully retained)

Important: the steward will never persist raw customer packets or complete HTTP bodies by default. There is a configurable "evidence-level" enum (minimal, enriched, full) per-customer with default=minimum.

Approval gate model:
- Preflight: run static validators (schema, delta size, risk heuristics) and estimate impact score.
- Operator signoff: operator selects one of: auto-commit, single-op-approval, multi-op-approval.
- Customer handshake: optionally require customer KMS co-sign via signed timestamp challenge.
- Canary / staged rollout: built-in step to delay full traffic shift until post-commit analytics validate NAT/route distribution.

Escalation policies (examples):
- Low risk (impact_score < 0.15): auto-approve and steward emits signed capsule; retention minimal.
- Medium risk: single operator approval required; steward marks capsule enriched.
- High risk (multi-segment change or sensitive subnet): multi-approval + customer co-sign.

Operator UX wireframe notes (Console):
- Compact review card showing: change summary, impact score, capsule size, required signers, ETA to commit.
- 'Evidence preview' panel that shows normalized diffs (redacted) and the canonical delta_hash.
- Inline policy link that lists which fields will be redacted and why.

Evidence capsule lifecycle and storage:
- Capsule creation: steward packages canonical-change-payload, normalized diffs, optional short traces (60s snapshot), and metadata.
- Short-term retention: capsule stored in customer-controlled bucket when present (preferred) or in Redwood short-ttl enclave (encrypt-with-customer-kms if requested).
- Archive: if customer opts-in, capsule is escrowed to immutable archive (signed manifest) with retention TTL defined in contract.

Forensics and replay helpers:
- Replay manifest: small JSON that points to each artifact and the order required to replay a change on a test harness.
- Deterministic replay: where possible, steward will provide deterministic, idempotent steps with checksums to reduce ambiguity during investigations.

Open failure modes / mitigations:
- Customer KMS unresponsive at co-sign time: steward marks transaction as 'co-sign-pending' and either holds commit (if policy mandates) or proceeds with advisory label.
- Capsule size > limit: steward attempts progressive trim (drop binary blobs, compress), then escalate to operator.
- Legal/subpoena: define contract path for how Redwood responds and whether capsules are considered customer data (recommendation: capsules are customer-owned when co-signed or stored in customer bucket).

Privacy & compliance notes:
- Default minimization: never store full IP packet payloads, user-identifying headers are hashed with salt.
- Jurisdictional constraints: if customer-region=EU, stewardship operations must not export capsule to non-EU storage unless explicitly allowed.
- Audit-proofing: every signature is time-bound and includes a small nonce to prevent replay attacks.

Rollout plan (high-level):
- Week 0–2: design reviews with infra, SRE, legal (agree on schema and ownership).
- Week 3–6: implement steward prototype + console wireframe + unit tests.
- Week 7–10: internal pilot with 2 infra customers + one sandboxed on-prem partner.
- Week 11–12: expand pilot and measure metrics, finalize contract language for co-signing.

Acceptance criteria (for initial pilot):
- Evidence capsule created and verifiably signed in 95% of pilot transactions.
- Average capsule <= 1 MB (or clear exception reason for oversized events).
- Customer KMS co-sign workflow completes within SLA 99% of attempts (or fallback behavior exercised and logged).
- Console shows capsule status and allows download of manifest and signed pointer.

Engineering & infra considerations:
- Minimal trusted codepath inside private control plane; keep steward small and auditable.
- Provide library bindings for canonicalization and signing so other teams (release-engineering, SRE) can create compatible capsules.
- Sampling: integrate with observability to decide when to keep enriched artifacts for later model-based anomaly detection.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Legal: are capsules customer-owned by default or does co-sign need to be present? Recommend: default to customer-ownership if co-signed or if stored in customer bucket.
- UX: how do we surface redactions to customers in a way that isn't confusing?
- Scope: does steward include application-layer change artifacts (API keys rotated) or limit to networking config?

Next steps / action items:
- PM: spawn CONFLUENCE design page that standardizes the capsule schema (owner: Leah).
- Infra: spike on customer KMS co-sign flow (owner: Ravi).
- Legal: draft short contract addendum for evidence escrow and co-sign (owner: Marta).
- Solutions: identify 3 pilot customers and draft runbook (owner: Owen).

Notes / references:
- See linked_artifacts for initial pointers to PR and ticket.
- Related concept: compact evidence capsule was briefly prototyped during onprem audit experiments (refer to audit-mini-envelope notes).

Comments (notes-to-self style):
- Keep steward's attack surface tiny — signing, packaging, pointer management. No query UI in steward itself.
- Think about a tiny CLI for customers to request on-demand co-sign for already-committed capsules.

Document status: quickdraft — needs a formal PRD and legal review.
